questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Whether gadgets are built not to last and why we throw them out
How to repair your own mobile phone at home with basic tools
The best new gadgets to buy this year and where to find them
How electronic waste is collected and recycled in Europe
questions.why: Neil asks if technology is built to fail and if we're throwing away too much and harming the planet.

questions.q: How old are Catherine's TV and mobile phone?
options: Both are brand new
Her TV is two and a half; her phone is five
Both are about ten years old
Her TV is five; her phone is about two and a half
questions.why: Catherine says her TV just had its fifth birthday and her phone is about two and a half.

questions.q: Why do people throw away so many gadgets, according to Neil?
options: They are too heavy and big to keep in the house
Recycling them is too difficult and takes too long
It often costs more to fix them than buy new ones
Shops refuse to repair them after the first year
questions.why: Neil says technology gets cheaper and many gadgets are more expensive to fix than replace.

questions.q: According to Professor Tim Cooper, what is the problem with mobile phone screens?
options: They are made of cheap plastic that scratches easily
They're glued in, so they can't easily be replaced
They are too big to fit comfortably in a pocket
They use too much battery when the light is bright
questions.why: He says screens are glued in; with a screw, consumers could replace a cracked screen themselves.

questions.q: Why does Professor Cooper think phone makers do this?
options: It makes the phones much cheaper to produce in factories
They want people to buy a new phone every year or two
Customers prefer phones with no screws on the back
It makes the phones stronger if they are dropped
questions.why: He says makers know screws would help phones last, but 'they want you to replace your mobile phone every year or two'.

questions.q: What example does Professor Cooper give about washing machines?
options: Modern ones last much longer than the old ones did
His own one broke down after just one year of use
They are now too expensive for most families to buy
His parents' lasted 37 years, but now they last 5–10
questions.why: He says his parents' washing machine lasted 37 years; these days they last between five and ten.

options: Buying better goods and labelling how long products should last
Banning cheap electronic products from shops across Europe
Only buying second-hand gadgets from friends and family
Keeping every phone for at least ten years before recycling
questions.why: He suggests buying higher quality if we can, and labels saying how long products are designed to last.

questions.q: What does Catherine plan to do with her phone?
options: Buy the latest model as soon as it comes out
Recycle it straight away at the local shop
Keep it and look after the screen carefully
Give it to Neil because he needs a new one
questions.why: She says she's happy with it but will protect the screen very carefully.
